purpose: Additive teaching fixes under the fast-path process (ADR-0029). Entries only add definitions, analysis dimensions, quantitative methods or named models; they never replace existing teaching. Each fix has one line in content-factory/RUN_LOG.md and every fixed node is checked by the T8 course gate's accuracy question.
rights_boundary: Revision-authored teaching supported by each node's registered promotion-eligible sources. No awarding-body wording.

methods.name: Profit
methods.formula: total revenue - total costs, where total costs = fixed costs + total variable costs
methods.worked_example: Revenue £50,000; fixed costs £12,000; variable costs £30,000. Total costs = £42,000, so profit = £50,000 - £42,000 = £8,000.
methods.interpretation: A negative result is a loss. Profit is a measure over a period and is not the same as the cash the business holds.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.1 Return on investment formula not taught

methods.name: Return on investment (ROI)
methods.formula: return from the investment / cost of the investment × 100
methods.worked_example: A £200,000 investment generates £30,000 profit in a year: ROI = £30,000 / £200,000 × 100 = 15% a year.
methods.interpretation: Compares the return with the resources committed. State which return (e.g. profit) and which period are used before comparing options.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.1 Operating profit and profit for the year formulas not taught

definitions: operating profit: gross profit less other operating expenses such as distribution and administrative costs; profit from trading before finance costs and tax
profit for the year: profit remaining after operating profit is reduced by net finance costs and taxation; available to retain in the business or distribute to owners

methods.name: Operating profit
methods.worked_example: Gross profit £400,000; distribution and administrative expenses £250,000. Operating profit = £400,000 - £250,000 = £150,000.
methods.interpretation: Shows how profitable the core trading activity is before financing decisions and tax.

methods.name: Profit for the year
methods.formula: operating profit - net finance costs - taxation
methods.worked_example: Operating profit £150,000; net finance costs £20,000; tax £26,000. Profit for the year = £150,000 - £20,000 - £26,000 = £104,000.
methods.interpretation: The profit attributable to owners for the period; it can be retained or paid out as dividends.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.2 Profit for the year margin formula not taught

methods.name: Profit for the year margin
methods.interpretation: The share of each £1 of revenue left for owners after all costs, interest and tax. Compare with gross and operating margins to see where costs are absorbed.

definitions: break-even chart: a graph with output on the horizontal axis and costs and revenue on the vertical axis, showing fixed costs, total costs and total revenue; break-even output is where the total revenue and total cost lines cross, and the horizontal distance between actual output and break-even output shows the margin of safety

fixes.run_log: 3.7.2 Statement of financial position not taught as a named statement

definitions: statement of financial position: a statement of a business's assets, liabilities and equity at a single point in time (often called the balance sheet); total assets equal total liabilities plus equity

fixes.run_log: 3.7.2 Payables days, receivables days and inventory turnover formulas not taught

methods.name: Payables days
methods.worked_example: Payables £60,000; cost of sales £730,000. Payables days = £60,000 / £730,000 × 365 = 30 days.
methods.interpretation: Average time taken to pay suppliers. A longer period helps cash flow but can strain supplier relationships or signal payment difficulty.

methods.name: Receivables days
methods.interpretation: Average time customers take to pay. A shorter period improves cash flow; compare with the credit terms the business offers.

methods.name: Inventory turnover
methods.formula: cost of sales / average inventories held
methods.worked_example: Cost of sales £730,000; average inventory £73,000. Inventory turnover = £730,000 / £73,000 = 10 times a year.
methods.interpretation: How many times inventory is used or sold and replaced in a year. Higher usually means inventory moves faster, but a sensible level depends on the industry.

definitions: venture capital: equity finance, often with management advice, provided by specialist investors to young or fast-growing businesses with high growth potential in exchange for a share of ownership; it brings expertise but dilutes control and investors expect a high return and an eventual exit

methods.name: Net gain
methods.formula: expected value of an option - cost of that option
methods.worked_example: Option A has an expected value of £500,000 and costs £350,000: net gain = £150,000. Option B has an expected value of £420,000 and costs £250,000: net gain = £170,000, so B has the higher net gain.
methods.interpretation: On financial grounds choose the option with the highest net gain, then weigh the reliability of the probabilities, risk attitude and non-financial factors.

methods.name: Market size
methods.formula: total sales of all firms in the market over a period, measured by value (revenue) or volume (units)
methods.worked_example: Three firms sell £2m, £3m and £5m in a year: market size = £10m by value.
methods.interpretation: Needed for market share and growth calculations. Value and volume can move differently when prices change.

fixes.run_log: 3.4.5 Inventory control chart, re-order quantity and influences on inventory levels missing

definitions: inventory control chart: a graph of inventory level over time showing the maximum inventory level, re-order level, buffer inventory, lead time and re-order quantity
re-order level: the inventory level at which a new order is placed
buffer inventory: the minimum inventory held as protection against unexpected demand or late delivery
lead time: the time between placing an order and receiving it
re-order quantity: the amount ordered each time inventory reaches the re-order level

methods.name: Re-order quantity
methods.worked_example: Maximum inventory 1,000 units and buffer inventory 200 units: re-order quantity = 800 units, so a delivery arriving at the buffer level restores the maximum.
methods.interpretation: Read from an inventory control chart as the vertical jump when a delivery arrives.

methods.name: Re-order level
methods.formula: buffer inventory + (usage per period × lead time in periods)
methods.worked_example: Buffer 200 units, usage 50 units a day, lead time 4 days: re-order level = 200 + (50 × 4) = 400 units.
methods.interpretation: Ordering at this level means the delivery should arrive as inventory falls to the buffer.

analysis_dimensions: influences on inventory levels: demand variability, lead time, supplier reliability, storage and holding costs, perishability or obsolescence, cost of stock-outs and the use of JIT

fixes.run_log: 3.6.2 Employee costs as a percentage of turnover and labour cost per unit formulas missing

methods.name: Employee costs as a percentage of turnover
methods.interpretation: The share of revenue spent on the workforce. A rising figure can mean pay has grown faster than sales or productivity has fallen.

methods.name: Labour cost per unit
methods.formula: total labour costs / units of output
methods.worked_example: Labour costs £300,000 for 60,000 units: labour cost per unit = £5.
methods.interpretation: Falls when productivity rises faster than pay. Compare over time or with competitors producing similar output.

fixes.run_log: 3.10.1 Kotter and Schlesinger methods of overcoming resistance not taught

models_frameworks: Kotter and Schlesinger's methods of overcoming resistance to change
definitions: education and communication: explaining the reasons for change so that people understand it; useful where resistance comes from misunderstanding, but slow with many people
participation and involvement: involving those affected in designing the change; builds commitment but takes time
facilitation and support: training, coaching or emotional support to help people adjust; helps where resistance comes from anxiety, but can be costly and may still fail
negotiation and agreement: offering incentives or concessions in exchange for accepting change; useful where a group clearly loses out, but can be expensive and invite others to negotiate
manipulation and co-option: selectively using information or giving resisters a token role; quick and cheap but can backfire if people feel manipulated
explicit and implicit coercion: forcing change through threats or authority; fast but risks resentment, and best reserved for urgent situations
